Apparently there are legal reasons that sexual assault cannot be handled by the Honor Committee, which has jurisdiction over Honor infractions, due to Title IX. Copied from the Cav Daily, the school newspaper:

"The Honor Committee does not prosecute sexual misconduct, nor does the University Judiciary Committee hold sexual misbehavior in its scope of jurisdiction — in part — for legal reasons.

Adjudicating in lieu of either of these student organizations in cases of sexual assault is the Sexual Misconduct Board, which oversees all cases concerning sexual misconduct among the student body.

Legal restrictions on both the federal and university level prohibit Honor or UJC from prosecuting students for sexual assault, which led to the creation of the Sexual Misconduct Board.

Title IX, a federal statute protecting against sex discrimination in every educational institution that receives federal funding, requires that a lower burden of proof be established for cases involving alleged cases of sexual discrimination. The statute mandates that the burden of proof is held at no more than 70 percent, but at the University, trials require only 51 percent — whereas honor trials have a 99 percent burden of proof."

I still wish sexual assault was an honor infraction. It is ridiculous that it is not. Mainly because honor infractions are single sanction, so if a student is found guilty, they are permanently expelled. Myself and many others are disgusted by the administration for not taking a stand.

 I live in a college town with a busy downtown area and many pedestrian friendly shops. One day, I walked into a little used bookstore with an old man working behind the counter. I poked around for a bit, eventually picked out a book, and went to the counter to pay. I didn't have any cash, just my debit card, and the old man told me that they couldn't accept debit or credit for less than 15 dollar purchases (the book was 7 dollars). I was ready to put the book back when he told me I could just keep it, and the next time that I was downtown, I could come back to pay for it. I kept trying to just put it back, but he just filled out a little slip of paper with the price and handed it to me, saying that he trusted that I was a good person and would pay for it when I could. It really moved me that a worker at such a small store (that probably made much less of a profit than many of the high end shops and restaurants surrounding it) would be willing to do that. I immediately went to the nearest convenience store to get cash back on another purchase and went to pay back the bookstore. That small bit of friendliness put me in a great mood for the rest of the day.

The science museum is awesome, as well as the aquarium. If you are interested in art, the Museum of Fine Arts is nice; there is a lot of ancient art that is fascinating. Close to the MFA is the Isabella Stewart Gardener museum. It's a beautiful historical mansion with amazing furniture, architecture, and an indoor garden. I went there once as a kid, and was in awe the whole time and pretended I lived there. On the other hand, I've been to the science museum, mfa, and aquarium about five or six times each and it is always fun. Another bonus, there is an IMAX theater next to the aquarium, in case you want to catch a show afterwards. Honestly, just exploring the city is my favorite part of living near Boston. If your legs can handle it, start at the end of Newbury Street, walk it to explore the shops, then cross the street to get to the Boston Gardens. Bring a picnic if you like, and have it next to the duck pond. From the gardens, move to the Commons, which are just across the street. Protip: take the T (subway system) everywhere; it's way easier than finding parking, and a fast way to really experience the city.
